name: Olo
catalog_quote: Neither length, stress or intonation are phonemic, but the following have been noted. ... Stress. Not phonemic. The first syllable in the word usually has slightly more stress than the following syllables. Only in one or two instances has the second syllable more stress than the first. e.g. /orou/ [o-ˈrou] 'leg'

audit.recode_to: fixed penultimate, non-strict (a few lexical antepenultimate exceptions), per Staley 2007 p.8; at minimum drop 'strict' and add a caution/contra entry citing Staley 2007 vs McGregor 1961/OPD 2004.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p.11 (PDF p.19) of the held PL D-42; confirmed from the page image. (2) Deciding source: a 13-page missionary phonemic statement written June 1961 (PL D-42 p. viii), published 1982; stress gets one impressionistic paragraph ('slightly more stress', 'not phonemic') and its examples are disyllables, where 'first syllable' and 'penultimate' coincide. (3) Better source exists and was not yet obtained: Staley 2007 (SIL e-Books 5, published version of a 1995 Oregon PhD by the SIL linguist resident from 1982), §2.2 p.8: 'Stress is mostly predictable, occurring on the penultimate syllable. There are a few words which have the antepenultimate syllable stressed', with the trisyllabic pair wai.kó.pou 'man's name' vs wá.ko.pou 'wooden pestle'. This directly contradicts 'fixed-strict initial': on trisyllables Staley's default is the penult and in
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. held, PDF p.19 = printed p.11 (text layer re-extracted): 'Stress. Not phonemic. The first syllable in the word usually has slightly more stress than the following syllables. Only in one or two instances has the second syllable more stress than the first. e.g. /orou/ [o-'rou] 'leg''. Verbatim as in the record's the domain quotation/sources; PL D-42 p.viii confirms the Phonemic Statement was prepared June 1961. No other stress statement anywhere in PL D-42 (a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned for stress/accent/emphasis; the grammar statement pp.15-80 only uses 'emphasis' for pronoun morphology). sources.quote: 'Stress is mostly predictable, occurring on the penultimate syllable. There are a few words which have the antepenultimate syllable stressed. A contrastive pair is given in (4). (4) wai.kó.pou 'man's name' / wá.ko.pou 'wooden pestle''
sources.note: Later description by the SIL linguist who worked on Olo 1982-1990s and compiled the dictionary; §2.2 p.8 says stress is penultimate with a few antepenultimate exceptions and gives a trisyllabic contrastive pair — contradicts our initial-stress coding, which rests on a 1961 missionary statement whose examples are disyllabic.
